Subject: school accounts

Hello,

Someone suggested I get in touch. We're an art and stationery shop and we supply a few local schools on account - they send a teacher or a TA in with a list, we make it up, and they take it away.

The way it's billed is the person at the till rings it through as a normal sale, prints the receipt, writes the school's name on it and staples it to a docket book page. The dockets build up.

Then at some point somebody types them into an invoice and emails it to the school office.

I say "somebody" and "at some point" because I'm not sure who does it or how often. It's not me. It might be my sister when she's in on Thursdays.

Schools take ages to pay anyway and some of them need a purchase order number on the invoice which we don't have because nobody asks for one at the till.

I don't know what's owed. I know it's a fair bit because one of the primaries asked us for a statement and we couldn't produce one.

Not sure what else to tell you. Happy to answer questions.

Subject: registering new patients

Hi,

You asked how a new patient gets onto our books.

They ring or come in. Reception hands them a clipboard with the registration form and the medical history questionnaire, and they fill it in sitting in the waiting room. It's four sides. Name, address, GP, medications, allergies, medical conditions, consent for us to hold their data, and the section about who's paying - NHS exempt, NHS paying, or private.

They hand it back, reception photocopies their exemption evidence if they've claimed exemption, and puts the form in a tray.

Later - same day if it's quiet, next day usually - reception types the details into SOE and creates the patient record. The paper goes in the filing cabinet.

Then they get an examination appointment, and the dentist reads the medical history off the screen.

Things that go wrong. People leave sections blank, especially the medications one, and nobody checks before they've gone. The handwriting on medications is often unreadable and the nurse ends up asking again in the surgery. Exemption evidence gets photocopied but nobody checks it's the right kind, and we've had claims rejected. And the form doesn't get typed up before the appointment sometimes, so the dentist is reading a paper form in the surgery.

Emma (Practice Manager)

CELLAR STOCKTAKE
Bar procedures, gastro pub

A stocktake of the cellar and back bar is performed weekly, on Sunday after close, to calculate gross profit on wet sales and identify losses.

The procedure states that the stocktake is carried out by the general manager alone, counting each line and entering the figures directly into the stock module, and that the assistant manager is not involved because the count must be done by the person accountable for the result.

Staff described a different arrangement, which they said has been in place all year: the general manager and the assistant manager count together, splitting the cellar between them - kegs and casks to one, bottles, wines and spirits to the other - and combining their sheets afterwards.

Both descriptions were given during the review as the current method.

Recorded difficulties: the two counters routinely disagree on part-used kegs, which are estimated by weight by one and by a dip stick by the other, and on spirits, which one counts by tenths of a bottle and the other to the nearest half. Combined sheets have shown the same line counted twice and other lines not counted at all. Where the resulting gross profit figure looks wrong, the figure is adjusted before it is reported to the owner rather than investigated. Wastage, staff drinks and promotional pours are not separately recorded, so any shortfall is attributed to theft or to "the count being out". No stocktake sheet from a previous week is retained for comparison.

gold.objective: Perform the weekly cellar and back bar stocktake to calculate gross profit on wet sales and identify losses.
gold.trigger: Sunday after close, weekly.

owner_and_participants.owner: Contradictory in input: the written procedure states the stocktake is carried out by the general manager alone, precisely because it must be done by the person accountable for the result, while staff describe the general manager and assistant manager counting together and splitting the cellar, and say this has been the arrangement all year - both were given as current
participants: The owner, to whom the gross profit figure is reported

inputs_data_required: Counted quantities for kegs, casks, bottles, wines and spirits
Part-used kegs, estimated by weight by one counter and by dip stick by the other
Spirits, counted to tenths of a bottle by one and to the nearest half by the other
systems_involved: A stock module into which figures are entered
current_process: A stocktake of the cellar and back bar is performed weekly on Sunday after close
The cellar is split between two counters - kegs and casks to one, bottles, wines and spirits to the other
Each counts their section and the sheets are combined afterwards
Figures are entered into the stock module and a gross profit figure is produced
Where the resulting gross profit figure looks wrong, it is adjusted before being reported to the owner
No stocktake sheet from a previous week is retained
bottlenecks_and_risks: Who performs the count is contradictory and both accounts are current - the procedure specifies the general manager alone so the accountable person does the count, while in practice the person being measured counts alongside the person he manages
Adjusting the gross profit figure when it looks wrong rather than investigating means the control is defeated by the person it is meant to measure

The two counters use incompatible methods on the same categories - part-used kegs by weight versus dip stick, spirits to tenths versus nearest half - so combining their sheets produces a figure with no consistent basis
Combined sheets have shown the same line counted twice and other lines not counted at all
Wastage, staff drinks and promotional pours are not separately recorded, so any shortfall is attributed to theft or a bad count - meaning genuine losses and legitimate usage are indistinguishable
No previous week's sheet is retained, so trends cannot be examined and the adjusted figures cannot be audited
recommended_improved_process: Resolve and document who counts, ensuring the count is not performed solely by the person accountable for the result
Define a single counting method per category - weight for part-used kegs, a consistent fraction for spirits - and train both counters on it
Use a structured count sheet listing every line so nothing is double-counted or missed
Record wastage, staff drinks and promotional pours separately so they can be excluded from loss
Prohibit adjustment of the gross profit figure; require investigation of variances instead
Retain every stocktake sheet and review trends over time
Have the owner review the unadjusted figure and the variance investigation
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can calculate expected stock from opening stock, deliveries and till sales, and compare it against the count to produce the variance
An AI agent can flag lines counted twice, lines not counted, and counts inconsistent with the defined method
An AI agent can trend variance by line and by week to distinguish recurring loss from count error
An AI agent can reconcile recorded wastage, staff drinks and promotional pours against the variance
human_approvals_controls: The owner receives the unadjusted gross profit figure; adjustments by the person being measured are prohibited
Counters sign their own count sheets and the combined sheet is verified by a second person
Variances above a threshold are investigated by a person and the investigation recorded
The owner approves the counting method and any change to it

CLIENT REVIEW MEETINGS
Note in agency operations folder

Each retained client is to have a monthly review meeting attended by the account lead, the relevant delivery specialists and the client.

Scheduling of these meetings is described below.

The account lead proposes dates to the client. Once the client indicates a preference, the account lead establishes whether the specialists needed can attend. A significant proportion of the delivery team are freelance and are engaged on a day-by-day basis; their availability is not held anywhere and changes from week to week, so each is contacted individually.

Where a required person cannot attend, either the meeting is moved, which requires the client to be approached again, or the meeting proceeds without them and questions are taken away.

Points noted at review: the number of meetings actually held against the number due was not available. Several clients were described as "we've not had one for a while" without a figure being attached. No agenda template exists and no notes or actions are recorded from the meetings. It was not established who is responsible for ensuring a meeting takes place, nor what happens when an account lead is on leave. No system holds the meeting schedule; invitations are sent from individual calendars. There is no standing time in the week reserved for these meetings.

gold.objective: Hold a monthly review meeting with each retained client, attended by the account lead, the relevant delivery specialists and the client.
gold.trigger: A monthly review is due for each retained client; the account lead proposes dates to the client.

recommended_improved_process: Hold a recurring monthly slot per client, booked in advance for the year
Maintain freelance and staff availability centrally so it can be checked without individual contact
Name an owner per client for ensuring the meeting happens, with defined cover during leave

Use a standard agenda template and record actions with owners and dates
Track meetings due, held and missed per client

Call notes - health and fitness club, member communications

- The club has a members' Facebook group with roughly 1,400 members. It was set up during a period of closure and was never wound down.
- Members post questions in it constantly: class timetable changes, is the pool open, is the sauna fixed, lost property, is anyone selling a spare place at the spin bike.
- Also complaints, sometimes at length and with photographs.
- Nobody is assigned to monitor or answer it. Three staff are admins - the fitness manager, a class instructor and a former duty manager who left last year and has not been removed.
- Answers are given by whichever member of staff happens to see a post on their own phone, in their own time. Instructors answer questions about the timetable that turn out to be wrong.
- Members answer each other, often incorrectly. A member told twenty others the pool was shut for a fortnight when it was two days.
- Nothing posted there reaches the club's actual systems. Lost property reports, maintenance issues and complaints raised in the group are not logged anywhere.
- The club also has an email address and a phone; posts in the group are not redirected to either.
- Response time, volume and themes are not measured.
- The owner reads it "occasionally, and it puts me in a bad mood".

gold.objective: Handle member questions and complaints posted in the club's Facebook group.
gold.trigger: A member posts a question or complaint in the Facebook group.

Discovery notes - online homeware brand, hiring a customer service assistant (call cut short)

- Business is recruiting its first customer service hire. Two previous attempts were described as unsuccessful.
- The advert was posted somewhere - Indeed was mentioned, then "or it might have been the Facebook page".
- Applications arrive at an address that was not identified. Volume not known.
- Shortlisting: someone reads them. Who, was not established.
- Candidates are sent a trial task: a set of sample customer emails to answer, returned by email.
- There is no marking scheme, no model answer and no list of what is being looked for. Asked how a good response is distinguished from a poor one, the answer was "you can just tell".
- Who reviews the task was not established; two different people were named at different points in the call.
- No record is kept of the tasks or the assessment.
- Whether candidates are told the outcome was not clear. It was accepted that some are not.
- Interview stage: exists, format not described.
- Reference and right to work checks: not discussed before the call ended.
- Salary: "we haven't decided".
- Nobody could say how long the previous two hiring rounds took or why the hires did not work out.

Kirsty: whose is the £412 at Plumbase yesterday

Report unallocated spend by engineer so the behaviour can be addressed
Verify that the control is operating rather than relying on it having been communicated

[Teams call - accountancy practice, two partners]

FIONA: The Bramhall complaint. Who's dealing with it?
RICHARD: I am. It's my client.
FIONA: It's a complaint about you missing their filing deadline.
RICHARD: Which is exactly why I should deal with it. I know the background.
FIONA: Do we have a procedure for this?
RICHARD: There's something in the manual. I've not looked at it.
FIONA: So what have you done?
RICHARD: Rung him, apologised, agreed to pay the penalty ourselves, and told him I'd waive this quarter's fee.
FIONA: Is any of that written down?
RICHARD: I made a note in my diary.
FIONA: Has anyone else in the practice seen it?
RICHARD: You have, now.
FIONA: How many of these have there been?
RICHARD: Complaints? A handful.
FIONA: Where would I find them?
RICHARD: They'd be with whoever the client belongs to.
FIONA: So there isn't a list.
RICHARD: There isn't a list.
FIONA: Our PII renewal asks whether we've had complaints in the year.
RICHARD: We say no.
FIONA: Do we.
RICHARD: We have said no.

Hi,

You asked about how we keep on top of safety certificates for the managed portfolio. We manage 340 properties.

Every property needs a gas safety certificate annually if it has gas, an EICR every five years, an EPC every ten, and smoke and CO alarm checks at the start of each tenancy. Some have oil instead of gas and need a different check.

Practice policy note, mixed small animal veterinary practice

The practice provides its own first-line out of hours cover between 19:00 and 08:00 and at weekends, with surgical and inpatient work referred to a dedicated emergency provider twelve miles away.

Arrangements as currently operated:

The practice answerphone message gives a mobile number. The mobile is held by the duty veterinary surgeon, who takes it home. The rota for who holds the phone is drawn up monthly by the practice manager and pinned in the staff room.

An owner calls and describes the animal's condition. The duty vet triages by telephone: advises, asks the owner to attend the practice, or directs them to the emergency provider. Where the owner is asked to attend, the duty vet drives in and a nurse is called in separately by the vet.

Points noted: the mobile number is a personal handset, not a practice line, and its call log is the only record of contact volume. Owners have kept the number and called it during working hours and on the vet's days off. There is no script or triage protocol, so advice for the same presentation differs between vets. Subject: conveyancing quotes

Hi,

You asked how we quote for a conveyancing job. It's mostly done on the phone and it's mostly done badly.

Someone rings up - a buyer, a seller, sometimes an estate agent on their behalf. Whoever answers takes the call. That could be me, could be one of the conveyancers, could be reception if we're stretched.

They ask the price, whether it's freehold or leasehold, whether there's a mortgage, whether it's a new build, and whether it's shared ownership. Then they give a fee.

Our fee scale is in a document on the shared drive and most of us roughly know it. The disbursements are the problem. Searches, Land Registry fees, SDLT, the leasehold pack, the management company fees on a leasehold - those get estimated from memory on the call. The leasehold ones especially, because the management pack can be £150 or it can be £600 and you don't know until you ask.

Then we email a confirmation, sometimes. Sometimes the first written thing they get is the client care letter a week later with a different number on it.

Clients get cross about that, understandably.

We don't know how many quotes we give or how many we win. The estate agents send us work partly on price and we've no idea whether we're cheap or dear.

Nothing's recorded. There's no quote log.

Richard

Call notes - independent garage, 4 ramps, MOT bay

Process: producing and communicating repair estimates.

- Trigger: a vehicle is booked in for diagnosis, or a fault is found during a service or MOT.
- The mechanic assesses the vehicle on the ramp and writes what is needed on the job card - a paper card that travels with the vehicle - in abbreviated form. Parts are described as "n/s front wishbone" or similar.
- The mechanic then either walks to the office and tells the receptionist, or the receptionist comes out to the workshop, or the job card is left on the desk.
- The receptionist prices it. She rings one or two parts factors for a price, adds labour at the hourly rate multiplied by whatever time the mechanic said, and adds VAT.
- She then phones the customer and gives a figure verbally. Nothing is sent in writing unless the customer asks, in which case she types it into an email.
- The customer's authorisation is verbal. It is noted on the job card as a tick and initials.
- Where further work is found once started, the same process happens again mid-job, and the vehicle sits on a ramp until the customer answers their phone.
- Labour times are the mechanic's estimate, not from a published time guide. The garage has a subscription to a technical data system that includes labour times; the receptionist said she does not have a login.
- No record of estimates given, accepted or declined is kept. Conversion is not known.

PARTS PROCUREMENT
Written procedure and note of review, independent garage

The procedure in the office folder states that all parts are ordered by the parts controller against a written parts requisition raised by the technician, that a single preferred factor is used for all routine items under a negotiated discount agreement, and that a goods received note is completed and matched to the invoice.

At review it was established that there is no parts controller and no requisition form. Technicians phone three factors themselves from the workshop, choosing whichever they think will have the part or deliver quickest, and give the vehicle registration over the phone. Whoever is nearest signs for the delivery. No goods received note exists.

Both the written procedure and the practice described were said by the workshop foreman to be "how it works", the procedure being what the garage's insurer was shown.

Recorded consequences: wrong parts are delivered frequently, estimated by the foreman at "a couple a week", usually because the registration was misheard or the vehicle has a mid-year variant. Wrong parts are returned, or not - a shelf of unreturned parts was observed and its value was not known. Discounts differ between the three factors and no one compares invoice prices against the discount agreed. Parts fitted are written on the job card but the supplier invoice is not matched to the job, so parts bought for one vehicle are sometimes charged to another. Monthly statements from the three factors are paid without line-by-line checking.

input:
Subject: warranty on parts

Hi,

Trying to explain this because it comes up a lot and it always ends badly.

We fit a part, say an alternator. Six months later it fails. Customer's back on the forecourt, not happy.

The part has a warranty from whoever made it, which we claim through the factor we bought it from. That covers the part. It doesn't cover our labour to take the old one off and put the new one on, usually. Sometimes it does if you argue.

So there's three of us in it - the customer, us, and the factor - and everyone thinks someone else should pay.

What happens is somebody has a phone conversation with the factor, and somebody has a different conversation with the customer, and those two conversations don't necessarily agree. Then the customer rings back and gets whoever answers, and that person doesn't know what was said.

I couldn't tell you who deals with these. It's not one person.

We don't have the original invoice to hand usually, so we're looking through job cards to find when we fitted it and what part it was.

I don't know how many we do a year or what they cost us in labour we don't get back. It's not recorded as anything, it just goes on the job as a nil charge.

Some customers get their labour free and some get charged and I don't think there's a reason for the difference.

Call notes - independent garage, customer communication and courtesy cars

- The garage has three courtesy cars. Demand exceeds supply in most weeks.
- Booking: a customer asks for one when they book the job in. The receptionist writes the registration and the date in a diary. There is no check that the car is back from the previous customer.
- Cars are returned with varying fuel levels and are not always cleaned or checked between users. Damage found is often not attributable because no condition check is done at handover.
- Insurance: drivers are added to the trade policy by phone. The receptionist said this "usually" happens before the customer drives away.
- Job progress: a customer rings to ask how their car is doing. The receptionist puts them on hold, walks into the workshop and shouts to the technician over the noise, then comes back with an answer.
- Where the technician is under a car or out on a road test, the customer is told someone will ring back. The callback is written on a sticky note.
- Completion: the customer is rung when the car is ready. Whoever is on reception does this from the job cards in the "done" pile. Cars have been finished for a day before the customer was told.
- Nothing is recorded about what the customer was told or when.
- No text or email updates are sent. The garage's management system can send them; nobody has set it up.
